column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: A doctor explains that a patient's cancer started in a single cell in the lining of the colon. What went wrong with that cell?
column14: It shrank and was broken down by the body
column15: It began dividing over and over without control
column16: It stopped dividing and could no longer be replaced
column17: It was infected by bacteria that spread through the colon
column28: Cancer starts when one cell loses control of the cell cycle and keeps dividing when it should stop. A common mistake is thinking cancer is an infection; bacteria do not cause the out-of-control division.
column29: Think about what the cell cycle normally controls.

column9: Cancer is a disease in which cells grow and ___ out of control.
column28: Cancer is uncontrolled cell growth and division. A common mistake is writing "die": cancer cells actually avoid dying when they should.
column29: What does a cell do during mitosis?

column9: Which cell process goes wrong in every type of cancer?
column14: Control of cell division
column15: Digestion of food in the cell
column16: Making energy by photosynthesis
column17: Osmosis across the cell membrane
column28: Every cancer is a problem with the control of cell division: cells keep going through the cell cycle when they should stop. Osmosis and digestion are unrelated, and human cells do not do photosynthesis.
column29: Cancer cells make too many copies of themselves.

column9: Which word names a lump or mass made of extra cells that have kept dividing?
column14: Spindle
column15: Chromosome
column16: Gamete
column17: Tumor
column28: A tumor is a mass of extra cells. Gametes are sex cells, chromosomes hold DNA, and the spindle moves chromosomes during mitosis.
column29: This is the word for the pile of extra cells.

column9: A dermatologist removes a small growth from a man's back. Lab tests show its cells stayed packed together in one spot and never entered the tissue around it. How should this growth be described?
column14: Carcinogenic
column15: Metastatic
column16: Benign
column17: Malignant
column28: A tumor that stays in one place and does not invade nearby tissue is benign, and it is not cancer. Malignant tumors invade, and metastatic means the cancer has already spread. Carcinogenic describes something that causes cancer, not a tumor.
column29: Did the growth spread or invade anything?

column9: Which word describes a tumor that is cancer because its cells can push into the tissue around it?
column14: Benign
column15: Malignant
column16: Dormant
column17: Haploid
column28: Malignant tumors invade nearby tissue and can spread, so they are cancer. Benign tumors stay put. Haploid describes gametes with one set of chromosomes, which has nothing to do with tumors.
column29: This is the dangerous kind of tumor.

column9: Cells from a woman's breast tumor are found growing in her hip bone. What word describes this?
column14: Apoptosis
column15: Mitosis
column16: Metastasis
column17: Differentiation
column28: When cancer cells break away and start new tumors in another part of the body, it is metastasis. Apoptosis is programmed cell death, which is the opposite of what cancer cells do. A common mistake is mixing up these two similar-sounding words.
column29: The cancer moved from where it started to a new place.

column9: Which body cells can become cancer cells?
column14: Almost any kind of body cell that can divide
column15: Only skin cells, because they get sunlight
column16: Only lung cells, because they breathe in smoke
column17: Only blood cells, because they travel around the body
column28: Cancer can start in almost any tissue that has dividing cells: skin, blood, breast, colon, lung, bone, and more. That is why there are so many kinds of cancer. Thinking cancer only happens in one organ is a common mistake.
column29: Think of how many different cancers you have heard of.

column9: A worker sanding old paint wears a mask because the dust contains a carcinogen. What can a carcinogen do?
column14: Cause DNA changes that can lead to cancer
column15: Help cells divide normally
column16: Give cells extra energy
column17: Cure cancer that has already formed
column28: A carcinogen is anything that causes the DNA mutations that can lead to cancer. It does not treat cancer. The mask lowers how much carcinogen reaches the lungs.
column29: The word itself contains "carcin-", which means cancer.

column9: Cell cycle checkpoints work most like which everyday thing?
column14: A gas pedal that keeps pushing a car to go faster down the road
column15: A security check that stops a traveler until everything is OK
column16: A copy machine that makes extra copies of a page
column17: A garbage truck that hauls broken things away
column28: A checkpoint stops the cell cycle until the cell passes inspection: DNA copied correctly, cell big enough, chromosomes attached. A gas pedal only speeds things up, which is the opposite of a checkpoint's job.
column29: Checkpoints decide whether the cell is allowed to go on.

column9: What is a mutation?
column14: A type of tumor
column15: A medicine used for cancer
column16: A change in a cell's DNA
column17: A new cell made by mitosis
column28: A mutation is a change in the DNA. Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle can lead to cancer. A mutation is not the tumor itself; it is the cause inside one cell.
column29: It happens to the cell's genetic instructions.

column9: What usually has to happen inside a cell before it becomes a cancer cell?
column14: Its DNA is copied perfectly with no changes at all
column15: Genes that control the cell cycle become mutated
column16: It switches from mitosis to meiosis to divide
column17: Its DNA leaves the nucleus and enters the cytoplasm
column28: Cancer starts with mutations in the genes that control when a cell divides. Perfect DNA copying is what prevents cancer. Cancer cells still divide by mitosis, not meiosis.
column29: Cancer is a problem with the cell's instructions for dividing.

column9: Why does wearing sunscreen lower your risk of skin cancer?
column14: It shrinks tumors so they can't grow on the skin
column15: It makes skin cells divide faster to replace burned ones
column16: It blocks UV rays that can damage the DNA in skin cells
column17: It kills any cancer cells that are already in the skin
column28: UV radiation is a carcinogen: it causes mutations in skin cell DNA. Blocking UV means fewer mutations. Sunscreen prevents damage; it does not treat cancer that is already there.
column29: Sunscreen stops something from reaching your skin.

column9: When a cell with badly damaged DNA destroys itself on purpose, the process is called ___.
column28: Apoptosis is programmed cell death. It protects the body by removing damaged cells before they can divide. A common mistake is writing metastasis, which is the spreading of cancer.
column29: It starts with "apo-" and is the cell's built-in self-destruct.

column9: Cancer cells can keep dividing even when the body does not need any new cells.
column28: True. Normal cells divide only when the body needs them (to grow or heal). Cancer cells ignore those signals and keep dividing.
column29: Do cancer cells follow the body's stop signals?

column9: Can a student catch cancer by sitting next to a classmate who has it?
column14: Yes, because cancer cells can float through the air in a room
column15: No, because cancer comes from changes in a person's own cells
column16: Only if the classmate coughs or sneezes on them
column17: Yes, because cancer can spread by touching someone's skin
column28: Cancer is not contagious. It starts when a person's own cells get mutations and divide out of control. A few viruses, like HPV, can raise cancer risk, but it is the virus that spreads, not the cancer.
column29: Where does a cancer cell come from in the first place?

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Cancer :: A disease of uncontrolled cell division
column15: Tumor :: A mass of extra cells
column16: Metastasis :: Cancer cells spreading to new parts of the body
column17: Carcinogen :: Something that causes cancer-causing DNA changes
column28: Cancer is the disease, a tumor is the mass of cells, metastasis is the spreading, and a carcinogen is a cause such as tobacco smoke. Mixing up metastasis and carcinogen is common because both are long, unfamiliar words.
column29: Start with the one you know best, then use "carcin-" = cancer to place carcinogen.

column9: Which of these are carcinogens? Select all that apply.
column14: Chewing tobacco
column15: Cigarette smoke
column16: Clean drinking water
column17: Ultraviolet (UV) light from tanning beds
column28: UV light, cigarette smoke, and chewing tobacco all cause DNA mutations that can lead to cancer. Apples, clean water, and sleep do not damage DNA. A common mistake is thinking only smoking (not chewing) tobacco is a risk.
column29: Which of these can damage the DNA in your cells?

column9: In the car analogy for the cell cycle, what does cancer look like?
column14: The car is parked with the engine turned off
column15: The car runs out of gas and coasts slowly to a stop at the curb
column16: The car stops at every red light and stop sign along the way
column17: The gas pedal is stuck down or the brakes don't work
column28: Go signals are the gas pedal and stop signals are the brakes. Cancer happens when the gas sticks on or the brakes fail, so the cell keeps dividing. A parked car would be a cell that never divides.
column29: Cancer cells keep going when they should stop.

column9: Radon gas, asbestos, and benzene can all cause DNA mutations that lead to cancer. Each is called a(n) ___.
column28: Anything that causes cancer-causing mutations is a carcinogen. A common mistake is writing "mutation": the mutation is the change in DNA, and the carcinogen is what causes it.
column29: The word starts with "carcin-".

column9: When cancer spreads, how do the cancer cells usually travel to other parts of the body?
column14: Along the hair
column15: In the air a person breathes out
column16: In sweat
column17: Through the blood and the lymph
column28: Cancer cells break off and travel in blood vessels or lymph vessels, then start new tumors. The lymph system is a set of vessels that carries fluid around the body, so it gives cancer cells a route too.
column29: Which body fluids flow through vessels to every organ?

column9: Which of these cells is acting most like a cancer cell?
column14: A cell that stops dividing when the tissue around it is full
column15: A damaged cell that destroys itself
column16: A nerve cell that rests and does not divide for many years
column17: A cell that ignores signals telling it to stop dividing
column28: Cancer cells ignore stop signals and keep dividing. The other three are normal, healthy behaviors: stopping when the tissue is full, resting, and self-destructing when damaged.
column29: Which cell is breaking the rules?

column9: Compared with normal cells in the same tissue, how do cancer cells usually divide?
column14: They never divide; they just grow larger
column15: Less often, so they build up slowly over many years
column16: Only once, and then they die right away
column17: More often, and they don't stop when they should
column28: Cancer cells divide again and again without control. A common mistake is thinking tumors grow because cells get bigger; they grow because there are more and more cells.
column29: A tumor is a pile of extra cells. Where did the extras come from?

column9: A small tumor is found early and has not spread. Which treatment is most likely to remove it?
column14: Surgery to cut the tumor out
column15: Antibiotics to kill the tumor
column16: A cast to hold the area still
column17: A flu shot to boost the immune system
column28: A tumor that is still in one place can often be removed with surgery. Antibiotics kill bacteria, and cancer is not a bacterial infection, which is a common mix-up.
column29: The tumor is all in one spot.

column9: Radiation therapy aims high-energy rays at a tumor. What do the rays do to the cancer cells?
column14: Damage their DNA so they can't keep dividing
column15: Give them extra energy until they burn out
column16: Push them into the blood so they leave the body
column17: Turn them back into healthy, normal cells
column28: Radiation breaks the DNA of cells in its path. Cells with badly broken DNA cannot divide and often die. That is why the rays are aimed only at the tumor.
column29: Radiation can damage DNA. Why would that hurt a tumor?

column9: Which choices lower a person's risk of getting cancer? Select all that apply.
column14: Wearing sunscreen outdoors
column15: Getting the HPV vaccine
column16: Smoking only on weekends
column17: Using a tanning bed every week
column28: Avoiding tobacco, blocking UV, and preventing HPV infection all mean fewer DNA mutations. Tanning beds give off UV, and any smoking exposes cells to carcinogens. A common mistake is thinking a little smoking is safe.
column29: Which choices reduce exposure to things that damage DNA?

column9: Cancer starts with changes (mutations) in a cell's DNA.
column28: True. Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle let a cell divide out of control. Every cell that comes from it carries the same mutation.
column29: What does a carcinogen damage?

column9: Match each term to what it describes.
column14: Benign tumor :: Stays in one spot and does not spread
column15: Malignant tumor :: Invades nearby tissue and can spread
column16: Metastasis :: Cancer cells start new tumors in a distant organ
column17: Apoptosis :: A damaged cell destroys itself on purpose
column28: Benign stays put, malignant invades, metastasis is the spreading, and apoptosis is programmed cell death. Mixing up apoptosis and metastasis is the most common mistake.
column29: Apoptosis is helpful; metastasis is harmful.

column9: Leukemia is a cancer of white blood cells. Where in the body does the out-of-control cell division start?
column14: In the hair follicles, where cells divide fast
column15: In the bone marrow, where blood cells are made
column16: In the skin, where it is exposed to sunlight
column17: In the stomach, where food is digested
column28: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, so leukemia starts there when blood-forming cells divide out of control. Cancer starts in the tissue where the cells are made.
column29: Where are new blood cells produced?

column9: Melanoma is a skin cancer often linked to bad sunburns. Which carcinogen is the main cause?
column14: Chlorine in swimming pool water
column15: Sweat that stays on the skin too long
column16: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun
column17: Cold air that dries out the skin
column28: UV radiation from the sun (and tanning beds) causes mutations in skin cells, which is why sunburns raise melanoma risk. Chlorine, sweat, and cold air do not cause the DNA mutations behind melanoma.
column29: What in sunlight causes a sunburn?

column9: Which habit is the leading cause of lung cancer?
column14: Drinking milk
column15: Smoking cigarettes
column16: Running
column17: Eating vegetables
column28: Tobacco smoke carries many carcinogens straight into the lungs, where they damage DNA. It is the number one cause of lung cancer.
column29: Which choice puts harmful chemicals into the lungs?

column9: Put these steps in order, from a healthy cell to a tumor.
column14: The mutation breaks a gene that controls the cell cycle
column15: The pile of extra cells forms a tumor
column16: A carcinogen damages the cell's DNA
column17: The mutated cell keeps dividing, and every new cell carries the mutation
column28: Damage comes first, then the broken control gene, then repeated division, and finally the tumor. A common mistake is putting the tumor before the dividing; the tumor is made of the extra cells.
column29: What has to happen before there are enough cells to form a lump?

column9: Which statement about tumors is true?
column14: Tumors can only form in the skin
column15: Some tumors are benign and are not cancer
column16: Tumors are made mostly of dead cells
column17: Every tumor is cancer and will spread
column28: Benign tumors are masses of extra cells that stay in place, so they are not cancer. Only malignant tumors are cancer. Tumors are living, dividing cells and can form in almost any tissue.
column29: There are two kinds of tumors.

column9: Normal, controlled cell division is useful. Which is an example of it?
column14: Cells in a lump keep dividing for months
column15: A mole keeps growing and changing shape
column16: Skin cells divide to heal a scrape, then stop
column17: Cells break off a tumor and travel in the blood
column28: Healing a scrape is controlled division: the cells divide only until the gap is filled, then stop. The other three are signs of out-of-control division.
column29: Look for the cells that know when to stop.

column9: Genes that act like the brakes of the cell cycle, slowing or stopping cell division, are called tumor ___ genes.
column28: Tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. When they are damaged, nothing stops the cell from dividing. A common mistake is mixing them up with proto-oncogenes, which are the gas pedal.
column29: These genes "press down" on tumors to keep them from forming.

column9: Which kind of normal gene acts like the gas pedal, telling a cell when it is time to divide?
column14: Proto-oncogene
column15: Carcinogen
column16: Gamete
column17: Tumor suppressor gene
column28: Proto-oncogenes are the gas pedal: they send go signals. Tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. A carcinogen is not a gene at all; it is a cause of mutations.
column29: The brakes are tumor suppressors. What is the other kind?

column9: A cell with a mutation divides by mitosis. What happens to the mutation?
column14: Mitosis removes the mutation
column15: The daughter cells turn back into normal cells
column16: Only the larger daughter cell gets it
column17: Both daughter cells get a copy of the mutation
column28: Mitosis copies all of the DNA, including mistakes, so both daughter cells carry the mutation. That is how one mutated cell becomes a whole tumor of mutated cells.
column29: Mitosis makes identical copies.

column9: At a checkpoint, a normal cell finds damage in its DNA. What does it try to do first?
column14: Travel into the blood
column15: Divide right away
column16: Form a tumor
column17: Stop and repair the DNA
column28: A checkpoint pauses the cell cycle so the damage can be repaired. If the damage is too great to fix, the cell goes through apoptosis. Dividing right away would copy the damage into new cells.
column29: A checkpoint is a stop sign, not a green light.

column9: Which of these is NOT true of cancer cells?
column14: They ignore signals telling them to stop dividing when crowded
column15: They destroy themselves when their DNA is badly damaged
column16: They divide again and again without control
column17: They can pile up and form a tumor
column28: Cancer cells avoid apoptosis; they keep living and dividing even with damaged DNA. Healthy cells are the ones that destroy themselves when the damage can't be fixed.
column29: Three of these describe cancer. Which one describes a healthy cell?

column9: Why do doctors encourage screenings like mammograms and colonoscopies?
column14: To make cells divide faster and heal
column15: To cause mutations that protect cells
column16: To find cancers early, before they spread
column17: To cure cancers by removing all mutations
column28: Screenings look for tumors while they are small and still in one place, when treatment works best. A screening finds cancer; it does not cure it.
column29: When is a tumor easiest to treat?

column9: A mole on someone's arm has suddenly started growing and changing shape. Why should a doctor check it?
column14: It is a bacterial infection
column15: Its cells may be dividing out of control
column16: Moles always disappear on their own
column17: Its cells have all died
column28: A mole that grows and changes is a warning sign that its cells may be dividing out of control, which can mean melanoma. Growth means more cells, not dead ones.
column29: Something that keeps growing has cells that keep dividing.

column9: Which statements about cancer are true? Select all that apply.
column14: It involves cells dividing out of control
column15: Every tumor is cancer
column16: It starts with mutations in DNA
column17: It is caused by bacteria
column18: Its cells can spread through the blood
column28: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division that starts with mutations and can spread through the blood. It is not a bacterial infection, and benign tumors are not cancer.
column29: Two of these are common myths.

column9: Which cancer risk factor can a person NOT control?
column14: The genes they inherited from their parents
column15: Whether or not they smoke cigarettes
column16: How often they use tanning beds
column17: Whether they wear sunscreen at the beach
column28: You cannot choose the genes you inherit, and some inherited mutations raise cancer risk. Smoking, sunscreen, and tanning beds are choices that change how much DNA damage a person gets.
column29: Which one was decided before you were born?

column9: One cancer cell divides into two. Then every new cell divides again. After 4 rounds of division, how many cancer cells are there?
column28: Each round doubles the number of cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16. A common mistake is multiplying 4 × 2 = 8 instead of doubling four times.
column29: Start with 1 and double it once for each round.

column9: What normally keeps healthy cells from dividing when the body doesn't need new cells?
column14: Running out of DNA to copy into new cells
column15: The nucleus bursting once the cell is full
column16: Stop signals and cell cycle checkpoints
column17: Carcinogens that slow down cell division
column28: The cell cycle is controlled by stop signals and checkpoints, the brakes. Carcinogens do the opposite: they damage DNA and can break those controls.
column29: Think of the brakes in the car analogy.

column9: Some chemotherapy drugs block mitosis. Why do these drugs harm cancer cells more than most normal cells?
column14: Cancer cells are much larger than normal cells, so they soak up more of the drug
column15: The drugs can only get inside cancer cells, never normal cells
column16: They divide more often, so more of them are in mitosis at any time
column17: Cancer cells have no DNA, so the drug breaks them apart easily
column28: A drug that blocks mitosis hits whatever cells are dividing. Cancer cells divide far more often than most body cells, so they are hit hardest. The drug does not recognize cancer cells; it targets division.
column29: The drug only works on cells that are dividing.

column9: Cells from a man's prostate tumor travel and form new tumors in his bones. What do doctors call the tumors in his bones?
column14: A bone infection caused by the tumor
column15: Prostate cancer that has spread to the bone
column16: A brand-new bone cancer that started in the bone cells
column17: Benign bone tumors that will not spread
column28: A cancer is named for where it started. The bone tumors are made of prostate cells that metastasized, so it is still prostate cancer. A common mistake is thinking every new tumor is a new cancer.
column29: What kind of cells make up the new tumors?

column9: A cell finishes copying its DNA, but one section was copied with mistakes. Which checkpoint should catch this before the cell starts mitosis?
column14: The M (spindle) checkpoint
column15: Cytokinesis
column16: The G2 checkpoint
column17: The G1 checkpoint
column28: The G2 checkpoint comes after the DNA is copied in S phase and before mitosis, so it checks the copying job. The G1 checkpoint comes before copying, and the M checkpoint checks chromosome attachment to the spindle.
column29: Which checkpoint comes right after S phase?

column9: During mitosis, a checkpoint makes sure every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers before the copies are pulled apart. What could happen if this checkpoint fails?
column14: The daughter cells could get the wrong number of chromosomes
column15: The cell would skip copying its DNA in S phase
column16: Nothing would change, since the DNA was already copied in S phase
column17: The cell would turn into a gamete instead
column28: If a chromosome is not attached, its copies may not split evenly, so one daughter cell gets an extra and the other is missing one. Wrong chromosome numbers can push cells toward cancer.
column29: What does the spindle do with the chromosomes?

column9: In a lab, normal skin cells spread into one flat layer and stop dividing once they touch each other. Cells from a tumor keep dividing and pile up into a heap. What does this show?
column14: Tumor cells ignore signals that normally stop cell division
column15: The normal cells died as soon as they touched
column16: Tumor cells divide more slowly than the normal cells next to them
column17: Tumor cells cannot carry out mitosis at all
column28: Touching neighbors is a stop signal for normal cells. The tumor cells kept dividing anyway, which is exactly the loss of control that defines cancer. A pile of cells means they kept doing mitosis, not that they stopped.
column29: Which cells obeyed the stop signal?

column9: A tumor cell divides once every day, and every new cell keeps dividing at the same rate. Starting from 1 cell, how many cells will there be after 10 days?
column28: The cells double every day: 2 × 2 × 2 … ten times = 2¹⁰ = 1,024. A common mistake is multiplying 10 × 2 = 20, which counts adding, not doubling.
column29: Double the number once for each day: 1, 2, 4, 8, …

column9: A student counts 200 cells on a slide of normal tissue and finds 10 of them in mitosis. What percent of the cells are dividing? (Enter just the number.)
column28: Percent dividing = 10 ÷ 200 × 100 = 5%. A common mistake is dividing 200 by 10 and getting 20.
column29: Divide the dividing cells by the total cells, then multiply by 100.

column9: Which of these describe cancer cells but NOT normal cells? Select all that apply.
column14: Keep dividing after they touch neighboring cells
column15: Avoid apoptosis when their DNA is badly damaged
column16: Have DNA inside a nucleus
column17: Can invade nearby tissue
column28: Ignoring crowding, invading tissue, and avoiding apoptosis set cancer cells apart. Normal body cells also divide by mitosis and keep DNA in a nucleus, so those do not tell them apart. A common mistake is thinking cancer cells use a different kind of division.
column29: Cross out anything that a healthy cell also does.

column9: A mutation in one of a person's skin cells leads to skin cancer. Why won't this mutation be passed to the person's future children?
column14: Children do not have skin genes
column15: Only mutations in the father's cells can be passed on to children
column16: Skin mutations fix themselves before the person reaches puberty
column17: It is in a body (somatic) cell, not in an egg or sperm
column28: Only mutations in gametes (egg and sperm) can be passed to children. A skin cell is a somatic cell, so its mutation is copied only to the skin cells that come from it by mitosis.
column29: Which cells actually go into making a baby?

column9: A woman inherits a mutated copy of BRCA1, a tumor suppressor gene, from her mother. What does this mean for her?
column14: Her breast cancer risk is higher, because every one of her cells starts with one brake damaged
column15: Her cells can no longer divide, because the brake gene is missing from them
column16: She definitely has breast cancer now, since one copy of the brake gene is already broken in every cell
column17: She can never get breast cancer, because she still has one working copy left
column28: An inherited broken tumor suppressor means one of the brakes is already damaged in every cell, so fewer new mutations are needed for a cell to lose control. Risk goes up, but cancer is not certain. A common mistake is thinking an inherited mutation means you already have cancer.
column29: Tumor suppressors are the brakes. She starts with one already broken.

column9: A classmate says, "Teenagers can't get cancer." Which response is most accurate?
column14: That's right, because cancer is caused by old age and nothing else
column15: That's right, because only adults have cells that are still dividing
column16: That's right, because teenagers' DNA is too new to have built up any mutations yet
column17: That's wrong; anyone can get cancer, but it is much more common in older adults
column28: Cancer can happen at any age because any dividing cell can get mutations. It is more common later in life because mutations build up over the years. Teenagers have lots of cell division going on, since they are still growing.
column29: Do teenagers' cells divide and copy DNA?

column9: Why does it usually take many years for lung cancer to develop after someone starts smoking?
column14: Smoke takes many years to travel all the way down into the lungs
column15: The body must form a tumor first, and only after that can the mutations start to happen
column16: Several mutations usually have to build up before a cell fully loses control
column17: Cancer cells divide only once a year, so tumors grow very slowly
column28: One mutation is usually not enough. A cell typically needs several hits to its gas-pedal and brake genes, and those take time to pile up. Smoke reaches the lungs right away.
column29: Is one mutation usually enough?

column9: Put these steps of metastasis in order.
column14: Cancer cells invade the tissue next to the tumor
column15: Cancer cells push into a blood or lymph vessel
column16: The cells travel through the body
column17: The cells leave the vessel and start a new tumor in another organ
column18: A tumor forms in the original organ
column28: Cancer must form a tumor, invade nearby tissue, get into a vessel, travel, and then settle in a new organ. A common mistake is putting travel before the cells have gotten into a vessel.
column29: The cells need a way in, a ride, and a way out.

column9: Put these events of the cell cycle in order, starting with a new cell.
column14: S phase: the DNA is copied
column15: G1 checkpoint: Is the cell big enough, and is its DNA undamaged?
column16: Cytokinesis splits the cell in two
column17: G2 checkpoint: Was the DNA copied correctly?
column18: M checkpoint: Is every chromosome attached to the spindle?
column28: G1 checkpoint → S (copy DNA) → G2 checkpoint → M checkpoint during mitosis → cytokinesis. The G2 checkpoint has to come after S phase, because it checks the copy. A common mistake is putting the G2 check before the DNA is copied.
column29: You can't check a copy until it has been made.

column9: Why do doctors aim radiation only at the tumor area instead of the whole body?
column14: Radiation makes tumors grow
column15: Radiation also harms healthy cells in its path
column16: Healthy cells cannot be hit by radiation
column17: Radiation only works on skin
column28: Radiation damages DNA in any cell it hits, healthy or not. Aiming it at the tumor kills cancer cells while sparing most healthy tissue.
column29: Does radiation know which cells are cancer cells?

column9: A benign tumor in the brain can still be dangerous. Why?
column14: It travels through the blood
column15: It will always spread to other organs through the blood
column16: As it grows, it can press on nearby brain tissue
column17: It is made of cancer cells
column28: Benign tumors don't invade or spread, but they still take up space. In the skull there is no room, so a growing mass presses on brain tissue. It is still not cancer.
column29: Think about space inside the skull.

column9: Why is cancer called a disease of the cell cycle?
column14: The cells no longer follow the normal controls on when to divide
column15: It is caused by cells skipping S phase and not copying their DNA first
column16: It is caused by germs that stop the cell cycle completely in every cell
column17: It only happens during meiosis, when gametes are made
column28: Cancer cells go through the cell cycle when they shouldn't because their checkpoints and stop signals are broken. They still copy DNA in S phase and divide by mitosis.
column29: What controls whether a cell divides?

column9: The HPV vaccine protects against a virus that can cause cervical and throat cancers. How does stopping this infection lower cancer risk?
column14: The virus can break the cell cycle controls in the cells it infects
column15: The vaccine stops every kind of mutation in the body
column16: The vaccine kills any tumors that have already formed
column17: The virus itself is a tumor that spreads from person to person by contact
column28: HPV makes proteins that switch off a cell's brakes, so infected cells can divide out of control. Preventing infection protects those controls. The vaccine prevents infection; it doesn't treat existing tumors.
column29: What does the virus do to the cells it infects?

column9: A scientist adds a chemical to normal cells in a dish. Weeks later, some of the cells keep dividing even after the dish is full. What is the best conclusion?
column14: The chemical fixed the cells' checkpoints so they work better
column15: The chemical is a vitamin that made the cells healthier, stronger, and faster growing
column16: The cells have died, and the heap is made of dead cells
column17: The chemical may be a carcinogen that mutated genes controlling the cell cycle
column28: Normal cells stop dividing when crowded. Cells that keep going have lost control of the cell cycle, which suggests the chemical caused mutations. Dividing cells are alive, not dead.
column29: What would normal cells do when the dish is full?

column9: Which change would be like cutting the brake lines of the cell cycle?
column14: A mutation that breaks a tumor suppressor gene
column15: A healthy, working checkpoint
column16: A mutation that makes a proto-oncogene stuck on
column17: A damaged cell going through apoptosis
column28: Tumor suppressor genes are the brakes, so breaking one is like cutting the brake lines. A proto-oncogene stuck on is a stuck gas pedal. Checkpoints and apoptosis are working safety systems.
column29: Brakes = genes that stop division.

column9: A gas-pedal gene that has mutated so it tells the cell to divide all the time is called a(n) ___.
column28: When a proto-oncogene mutates and gets stuck on, it becomes an oncogene. A common mistake is writing tumor suppressor, which is a brake gene, not a gas pedal.
column29: Take "proto-" off the name of the normal gas-pedal gene.

column9: Chemotherapy can cause side effects in tissues where normal cells divide often. Which tissues are likely to be affected? Select all that apply.
column14: Bone marrow, where blood cells are made
column15: Hair follicles
column16: Mature nerve cells in the brain
column17: The lining of the stomach and intestines
column28: Chemotherapy attacks dividing cells, so fast-dividing tissues like hair follicles, the gut lining, and bone marrow are hit. That causes hair loss, nausea, and low blood counts. Mature nerve and heart muscle cells rarely divide, so they are mostly spared.
column29: Which tissues are always making new cells?

column9: Two tissue samples come from the same organ. In Sample A, 2% of the cells are in mitosis. In Sample B, 30% are in mitosis. Which sample is most likely from a tumor?
column14: Sample A, because fewer cells are dividing
column15: Both, because all tissue divides the same
column16: Sample B, because far more of its cells are dividing
column17: Neither, because tumor cells don't do mitosis like normal cells
column28: Tumor cells divide out of control, so a much larger share of them are in mitosis at any moment. A low percentage is typical of normal tissue.
column29: Which sample has more cells dividing?

column9: A cell's G1 checkpoint is working normally. The cell is still too small, and nutrients are low. What will the cell do?
column14: Copy its DNA right away
column15: Break off and travel in the blood
column16: Start mitosis immediately
column17: Wait and not copy its DNA yet
column28: The G1 checkpoint lets a cell move on to S phase only when it is big enough and conditions are good. Otherwise it waits. Skipping this check is what cancer cells do.
column29: A checkpoint that works says "not yet."

column9: A long-time smoker's lung cells are exposed to carcinogens every day. Why does daily exposure raise cancer risk so much?
column14: Smoke kills every lung cell right away, and the dead cells turn into tumors
column15: Smoke contains sugar that feeds cancer cells and makes them grow faster
column16: Smoke makes the lungs grow bigger every year, so there are more cells that could become cancer
column17: Each exposure can cause new mutations, so the chance of hitting cell-cycle genes keeps rising
column28: Every exposure is another chance for DNA damage. The more mutations pile up, the more likely one cell gets hits in its gas-pedal and brake genes. If smoke killed every cell at once there would be no dividing cells to become cancer.
column29: More exposure means more of what?

column9: How does mitosis in a cancer cell compare with mitosis in a normal cell?
column14: The steps are the same, but cancer cells do it too often and without control
column15: Cancer cells skip prophase, so their chromosomes never condense or become visible
column16: Cancer cells use a completely different set of phases from the ones normal cells use
column17: Cancer cells make four daughter cells each time instead of two
column28: Cancer cells go through prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase just like normal cells. The problem is when and how often they divide, not how. A common mistake is thinking cancer uses a different kind of division.
column29: Is the problem how the cell divides, or when it divides?

column9: In one study group, long-time smokers got lung cancer at a rate of 15 per 1,000 people. People who never smoked got it at a rate of 1 per 1,000. How many times higher was the smokers' rate?
column28: 15 ÷ 1 = 15 times higher. A common mistake is subtracting (15 − 1 = 14), which gives the difference, not how many times larger.
column29: "How many times" means divide one rate by the other.

column9: Why is cancer often described as many different diseases instead of one?
column14: It can start in many tissues, from different mutations, and each kind behaves differently
column15: Every cancer is caused by a different germ that infects a different organ
column16: Only one organ can really get cancer, but doctors give it many different names by location
column17: Each cancer uses its own special kind of cell division instead of mitosis
column28: All cancers share uncontrolled cell division, but a lung cancer, a leukemia, and a melanoma start in different cells, have different mutations, and need different treatments. Cancer is not caused by germs, and it still uses mitosis.
column29: Think about how many tissues have dividing cells.

column9: Skin cancer is much more common on the face, ears, and back of the neck than on the soles of the feet. What is the best explanation?
column14: Cancer cells are attracted to the parts of the body closest to the brain
column15: The soles of the feet have no cells that divide, so they can't get cancer at all
column16: Those areas get the most UV exposure, so their cells get the most DNA damage
column17: Skin on the face has different DNA than skin on the feet
column28: UV radiation is a carcinogen. Skin that is in the sun the most collects the most UV-caused mutations. Every skin cell has the same DNA, and foot skin divides too; it just gets little sun.
column29: Which body parts are in the sun the most?

column9: A tumor is removed by surgery, but a few cancer cells had already slipped into the bloodstream. What could happen months later?
column14: New tumors could appear in other organs because the escaped cells keep dividing
column15: Nothing, because removing the tumor also removes every single cancer cell in the body
column16: The escaped cells would turn back into normal cells in the blood
column17: The escaped cells would become benign once they leave the tumor
column28: The escaped cells still carry their mutations, so they can keep dividing wherever they land and form new tumors. This is why doctors check lymph nodes and sometimes add chemotherapy after surgery.
column29: Do the escaped cells still have their mutations?

column9: The protein p53 stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger the cell to destroy itself. If both copies of a cell's p53 gene are mutated so the protein no longer works, what is most likely?
column14: The cell turns into a gamete and leaves the tissue
column15: The cell stops dividing forever because its brake is stuck on
column16: Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing and pass the damage on
column17: The cell repairs its DNA faster without p53 in the way
column28: p53 is a tumor suppressor (a brake). Without it, damaged cells are neither paused nor removed, so they divide and copy the damage into new cells. That is why p53 is broken in about half of human cancers. A common mistake is thinking a broken brake stops the cell.
column29: What happens to a car when its brakes stop working?

column9: A tumor doubles its number of cells every 3 months. It has 1 million cells now. If it keeps doubling at the same rate, how many million cells will it have 1 year from now? (Enter the number of millions.)
column28: 1 year = 12 months, which is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 doublings: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 million. A common mistake is doubling 12 times (once per month) or multiplying 1 × 4 = 4.
column29: First find how many doublings fit into 12 months.

column9: A tumor about 1 cm wide holds roughly 1 billion (1,000,000,000) cells. What is the smallest number of doublings needed for 1 cell to reach at least 1 billion cells? (Hint: 2¹⁰ is about 1,000.)
column28: 2¹⁰ ≈ 1,000, 2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000, and 2³⁰ ≈ 1,070,000,000. 29 doublings gives only about 537 million, so 30 is the smallest number. A common mistake is guessing 1 billion ÷ 2. This also shows a tumor can be big enough to find only after about 30 rounds of uncontrolled division.
column29: Every 10 doublings multiplies the cells by about 1,000.

column9: A tumor usually can't grow wider than about 2 millimeters unless it grows its own new blood vessels. Why might a drug that blocks new blood vessel growth slow the cancer?
column14: The drug would repair the mutations in the tumor cells' DNA
column15: The drug would turn the malignant tumor into a benign one
column16: The inner tumor cells would not get enough oxygen and nutrients to keep dividing
column17: The blood vessels are made of cancer cells, so the drug kills them along with the tumor
column28: Dividing cells need oxygen and nutrients delivered by blood. Without new vessels, a tumor runs out of supplies and stalls. The drug does not fix the mutations, and the blood vessels are normal cells that the tumor recruits.
column29: What does blood bring to every cell?

column9: Retinoblastoma is an eye cancer in young children. Children who inherit one broken copy of a tumor suppressor gene called RB often get tumors in both eyes. Children who did not inherit a broken copy rarely do. What is the best explanation?
column14: Tumor cells from the first eye always travel to the second eye in inherited cases
column15: Eye cells never divide in young children, so only inherited cases can get tumors
column16: RB is a gas-pedal gene, so one stuck copy is enough in the children who inherit it
column17: Each of their cells already has one broken copy, so only one more hit is needed
column28: A cell has two copies of each tumor suppressor, and both usually must be broken before the brake fails. Children who inherit one broken copy need just one more hit in an eye cell, so tumors are much more likely, even in both eyes. Others need two separate hits in the same cell, which is rare.
column29: How many copies of the brake gene does a cell have, and how many are already broken?

column9: Usually one mutated copy of a gas-pedal gene is enough to push a cell to divide, but both copies of a brake gene must be broken. Which picture explains this best?
column14: A car only speeds up when both of its gas pedals are stuck down at once
column15: One stuck gas pedal speeds up the car, but a car with two sets of brakes can still stop until both fail
column16: Brakes matter less than gas pedals, so a cell simply ignores one broken brake
column17: Gas pedals and brakes always fail at the same time, so both must be broken together
column28: An oncogene acts like a gas pedal stuck down: one copy is enough to keep sending go signals. A tumor suppressor is a brake; if one copy works, it can still stop the cell, so both must be lost. This is why oncogenes act after one hit and tumor suppressors usually need two.
column29: Think about what one working copy of each gene can still do.

column9: Scientists compare two lines of cells. Line X has a mutation that disables its G1 checkpoint; Line Y is normal. Both are exposed to the same UV light. Two days later, what result is most likely?
column14: Line Y forms more mutated cells, because its working G1 checkpoint keeps any repair from happening
column15: Neither line changes, because UV light cannot reach the DNA inside a nucleus
column16: Both lines stop dividing forever, because UV light destroys every cell it hits
column17: Line X keeps dividing with damaged DNA, while Line Y pauses to repair or its damaged cells die
column28: A working G1 checkpoint stops damaged cells so they can be repaired or removed by apoptosis. Without it, Line X copies the damaged DNA and divides, so mutations spread through its cells. A common mistake is thinking the checkpoint causes damage instead of catching it.
column29: Which line has a working stop sign?

column9: A website says, "Cancer just means cells dividing fast, so a slow-growing tumor can't be cancer." What is the best response?
column14: Wrong: cancer means losing control of division, and some cancers grow slowly
column15: Right: slow-growing tumors are always benign and can never spread
column16: Wrong: cancer cells never divide at all, so the speed of a tumor has nothing to do with it
column17: Right: every cancer grows fast, so a slow-growing tumor must be harmless
column28: What makes a tumor cancer is that its cells ignore the controls on division and can invade and spread. Some cancers, like many prostate cancers, grow slowly for years. Speed alone does not decide it, and cancer cells definitely divide.
column29: What separates a malignant tumor from a benign one?

column9: A cell has badly damaged DNA. Which of these would let it keep dividing anyway? Select all that apply.
column14: It obeys a stop signal from its neighbors
column15: Its p53 gene is mutated
column16: Its G1 checkpoint stops working
column17: Its DNA repair enzymes work normally
column18: It is unable to go through apoptosis
column28: A broken checkpoint, a broken p53, or a blocked apoptosis all remove a safety system, so the damaged cell can keep dividing. Working repair enzymes and obeying stop signals are protections that would prevent it.
column29: Pick the changes that remove a safety system.

column9: Put these from earliest to most advanced stage of cancer.
column14: The cancer has spread to distant organs
column15: A single cell has mutations in its cell-cycle genes
column16: A small malignant tumor is still in its original tissue
column17: Cancer cells are found in lymph nodes near the tumor
column28: Cancer begins with mutations in one cell, grows into a local tumor, reaches nearby lymph nodes, and finally metastasizes to distant organs. Each step means more spread and harder treatment. A common mistake is putting the lymph nodes after distant organs; nearby nodes are usually reached first.
column29: Think about how far the cancer has traveled at each step.

column9: Cancers that start from mature nerve cells are very rare in adults, but skin cancers are common. What is the best explanation?
column14: Mature nerve cells have no DNA, so carcinogens have nothing to damage
column15: Mature nerve cells rarely divide, so they have few chances to lose control
column16: Nerve cells go through apoptosis every day, so damaged ones never last long enough to divide
column17: The skull blocks all carcinogens from ever reaching the nerve cells
column28: Cancer is out-of-control division, and mutations get copied each time DNA is copied. Cells that rarely divide have few chances to become cancer. Skin cells divide constantly and get UV exposure, so they have many chances. Most brain tumors come from other, dividing support cells.
column29: Which cells go through the cell cycle more often?

column9: A student tests whether sunscreen protects yeast from UV damage. She puts sunscreen on clear plastic over one plate of yeast and shines a UV lamp on it for 30 seconds. Which is the best control plate?
column14: A different kind of yeast with sunscreen, under the same UV for 30 seconds
column15: The same yeast with sunscreen, under the same UV lamp for 2 minutes instead of only 30 seconds
column16: No control plate, since you can just see whether the sunscreen yeast survives
column17: The same yeast with plain clear plastic and no sunscreen, under the same UV for 30 seconds
column28: A good control changes only one thing, the sunscreen. Same yeast, same plastic, same lamp, same time. Changing the yeast type or the time adds a second variable, so you couldn't tell what caused the result.
column29: A control should match the test in every way but one.

column9: A large study found that people who used tanning beds before age 35 had a much higher rate of melanoma than people who never did. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Everyone who uses a tanning bed will get melanoma
column15: Tanning beds only harm people over 35
column16: Melanoma is contagious in tanning salons
column17: UV from tanning beds raises the risk of melanoma
column28: Higher rates in users support that tanning-bed UV is a carcinogen that raises risk. Higher risk is not certainty, so not every user gets melanoma. The study looked at use before 35, which says nothing about tanning beds being safe for older people.
column29: Does higher risk mean it will definitely happen?

column9: Cancer cells taken from a patient in 1951 are still dividing in labs today. Normal human cells in a dish stop dividing after about 50 divisions. What does this show?
column14: Normal cells divide faster than cancer cells, so they wear out sooner
column15: Cancer cells have lost the normal limit on how many times a cell can divide
column16: Normal cells in a dish turn into cancer cells after 50 divisions
column17: The cells taken in 1951 must not really be human cells anymore
column28: Normal cells have a built-in limit and eventually stop dividing. Cancer cells can keep dividing indefinitely, one more way they escape the normal controls. A common mistake is thinking the difference is speed rather than control.
column29: Which cells obeyed a limit?

column9: A pathologist studies a tumor sample. Which findings suggest the tumor is malignant rather than benign? Select all that apply.
column14: A smooth capsule surrounds the tumor and keeps it in one spot
column15: Tumor cells are pushing into the tissue next to it
column16: Tumor cells are found in a nearby lymph node
column17: The cells look just like the normal tissue around them
column18: Many cells are in mitosis and their nuclei have odd shapes
column28: Invading nearby tissue, reaching lymph nodes, and lots of abnormal-looking dividing cells are signs of cancer. A tumor that is walled off in a capsule with normal-looking cells is typical of a benign tumor.
column29: Malignant tumors invade and spread; benign tumors stay walled off.

column9: A new drug blocks the signal from an oncogene that keeps telling a cell to divide. In the car analogy, what is the drug trying to do?
column14: Turn on the car's headlights
column15: Repair a set of broken brakes
column16: Press harder on the gas pedal
column17: Take the foot off a stuck gas pedal
column28: An oncogene is a gas pedal stuck down. Blocking its signal removes the push to divide. Repairing the brakes would mean fixing a tumor suppressor, which is a different target.
column29: Oncogene = gas pedal or brakes?

column9: A cell's spindle checkpoint fails. One daughter cell gets an extra copy of a chromosome, and the other is missing one. How could this lead to cancer?
column14: Extra or missing chromosomes always make the cell die right away, so it can only ever lead to cancer by pure luck
column15: Chromosome number has nothing to do with which genes a cell has, so it changes nothing
column16: Missing a chromosome makes a cell divide more carefully at every checkpoint after that
column17: The cells now have the wrong number of copies of cell-cycle genes, like extra gas-pedal or missing brake genes
column28: Chromosomes carry genes. Extra copies of gas-pedal genes or missing brake genes upset the balance that controls division, which can push a cell toward cancer. A common mistake is thinking chromosome number doesn't affect the genes a cell has.
column29: What do chromosomes carry?

column9: All the cells in a person's skin tumor share the same mutation, but the person's blood cells do not have it. What does this tell you about the mutation?
column14: It arose in one skin cell during the person's life, and mitosis copied it into that cell's offspring
column15: It started in the person's blood cells and then moved through the bloodstream to settle in the skin cells
column16: It was inherited from a parent, so it was in the egg or sperm the person came from
column17: It happened during meiosis in the skin cells, when they were making new skin
column28: An inherited mutation would be in every cell, including blood cells. Since only the tumor has it, it arose in one skin cell, and mitosis copied it into every cell of the tumor. Skin cells don't do meiosis.
column29: If it were inherited, which cells would have it?

column9: Which lab result would best show that a chemical is a carcinogen and not just a poison?
column14: Exposed cells shrink and stop dividing for good
column15: Exposed cells survive, pick up mutations, and start dividing without control
column16: Exposed cells change color but keep acting like normal cells and dividing on schedule
column17: Every exposed cell dies within an hour of touching the chemical
column28: A poison simply kills cells. A carcinogen causes mutations that let cells keep dividing out of control, so the evidence is surviving cells with new mutations and uncontrolled growth. Dead cells cannot become cancer.
column29: Can a dead cell become a tumor?

column9: A friend says, "If I eat healthy and never smoke, I can't get cancer." What is the most accurate response?
column14: Only people who smoke ever get cancer, so not smoking is all you need to do
column15: Healthy choices lower risk, but DNA copying mistakes and inherited genes still matter
column16: Healthy choices make no difference, because cancer is decided only by the genes you inherit
column17: That's true; diet and smoking are the only things that cause DNA mutations
column28: Avoiding carcinogens cuts down DNA damage and lowers risk a lot. But every time DNA is copied there is a small chance of a mistake, and some people inherit mutations. So risk goes down but never to zero. Both extremes in the other answers are common mistakes.
column29: Are carcinogens the only way DNA can change?

column9: A tumor's cells have both an oncogene and a broken tumor suppressor gene. Why is this combination worse than either one alone?
column14: Having both makes the tumor benign, so its cells can no longer spread to other organs
column15: The two mutations cancel each other out, so the cell goes back to acting normal
column16: Having both makes the cells switch from mitosis to meiosis
column17: The gas is stuck on and the brakes are gone, so nothing slows the cell down
column28: An oncogene keeps pushing the cell to divide, and a broken tumor suppressor removes a way to stop it. Together, the cell has a strong go signal and no stop. Most cancers have several of these mutations, which is why many hits are needed.
column29: Think about a car with a stuck gas pedal AND no brakes.

column9: Chemotherapy is often given in rounds, with a few weeks of rest between doses. What is the best reason for the rest?
column14: It gives the tumor time to turn benign before the next dose is given
column15: It gives the cancer cells time to heal and grow back so the next dose works even better
column16: It lets healthy fast-dividing cells, like those in bone marrow, recover between doses
column17: The drug only works every few weeks, so extra doses would do nothing
column28: Chemo also hits healthy cells that divide quickly. Bone marrow makes blood cells, so it needs time to rebuild between rounds. Cancer cells usually recover less well, so each round shrinks the tumor more. The rest is for the patient's healthy tissue, not the cancer.
column29: Which healthy tissues does chemo also damage?

column9: Why is finding cancer cells in a patient's lymph nodes a warning sign that the cancer may reach other organs?
column14: Lymph nodes make carcinogens, which then cause new mutations in the organs nearby
column15: Lymph nodes are where all tumors first start, so finding cells there means a brand-new tumor
column16: Lymph vessels connect throughout the body and empty into the blood, giving cancer cells a route to distant organs
column17: Cancer cells in lymph nodes divide faster than anywhere else, so they spread on their own
column28: Cancer cells in a lymph node have already escaped the original tumor and entered a vessel system. Lymph eventually drains into the blood, which reaches every organ. That is why doctors check lymph nodes to decide how far a cancer has spread.
column29: Where does lymph fluid end up?

column9: UV light damages a skin cell's DNA while the cell is in G1. Why is it better for the cell to catch this at the G1 checkpoint than at the G2 checkpoint?
column14: DNA is only copied after mitosis, so the G2 checkpoint is too late to check anything
column15: At G1 the damage hasn't been copied yet, so it can be fixed before S phase copies it
column16: Damage caught at G2 is always repaired perfectly, so catching it early adds nothing
column17: The G2 checkpoint can't detect DNA damage at all; it only checks whether the cell is big enough
column28: S phase copies the DNA, including any damage. Catching the damage in G1 means it is repaired before copying, so the mistake isn't locked into both copies. A common mistake is thinking DNA is copied after mitosis; it is copied before.
column29: Which phase comes between G1 and G2, and what happens in it?

column9: In a lab study, 40 of 50 mice exposed to Chemical X developed tumors, while 3 of 50 unexposed mice did. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Chemical X prevents cancer, since some exposed mice stayed healthy
column15: Mice that are not exposed to Chemical X can never get tumors
column16: Chemical X greatly raised tumor risk in mice and is likely a carcinogen
column17: Chemical X causes tumors in every animal that is exposed to it
column28: 80% of exposed mice got tumors compared with 6% of unexposed mice, which strongly suggests Chemical X causes cancer. Not every exposed mouse got a tumor, and a few unexposed mice did, so the answers that say "every" or "never" go too far.
column29: Compare the two groups, but watch out for words like "every" and "never."
